To ask for a size, try things on and say whether they fit.

After the trip to the Turda Gorge, Nora knows Mrs Pop was right: it’s very cold in the mountains. On Monday afternoon she goes with Ana to a clothes shop in the centre.
Good afternoon! Can I help you with anything?
Good afternoon! I’m looking for a winter coat. A warm, long one.
We have these models. The grey one is wool, the black one is thinner. And we also have a green one, the colour of fir trees.
The colour of the green coat is gorgeous! Can I try it on?
Of course. The fitting room is at the back of the shop, next to the mirror.
The sleeves are a little too long. And it’s loose at the shoulders. Do you have a smaller size?
We have S. Here you are. And it’s on sale: forty per cent off.
Now it fits perfectly! I’ll take it. Ana, what do you think? Does the colour go with my eyes?
Perfectly. And look, this red scarf is ideal with the coat. I want to buy something for my sister too. Her birthday is on Friday.
Then get her these grey gloves. They’re as warm as my coat!
to help: “vă pot ajuta?” = can I help you?
to look for: eu caut (I look for)
to wear: dumneavoastră purtați (you wear, formal)
to try on: “să-l probez” = to try it on
“cum îți vine?” = how does it fit you?
to take: “îl iau” = I’ll take it (buy it)
to buy: “să-i cumpăr” = to buy for her
The genitive ending “-ului” has short syllables: “pal-to-nu-lui”. The “u” and “i” are joined: “-lui” sounds like a short “lui”.
In the feminine: “Anei” = “A-nei”, “bunicii” = “bu-ni-cii” (two “i”s at the end, the second barely heard).
Watch “â” and “ă”: “mâneci” (sleeves) and “mănuși” (gloves) sound similar but have different vowels.
“cămașă”, “mănuși”: the “ș” is clear, like “sh”. Without the comma, “camasa” is no longer correct.
“A purta” means “to wear” (clothes, glasses, a size). Watch the vowel change: port, porți, poartă.
In winter I wear a thick coat.
She is wearing a blue dress.
For “to put on” you say “a se îmbrăca” (to get dressed) or “a-și pune”: “Îmi pun geaca.” (I put on my jacket.)
I’m looking for a winter jacket.
It fits me well. (it’s the right size)
Do you have a bigger / smaller size?
For shoes you ask “Ce număr purtați?” (what number), not “ce mărime”.
The genitive shows possession (“whose?”). In Romanian, the owner takes a special ending attached at the end: -ului, -ei, -lor. The thing owned comes first and has the article.
The short rule: masculine and neuter nouns take -ului; feminine nouns take -ei or -ii (the genitive form looks like the plural: fete → fetei, bunici → bunicii); the plural takes -lor.
Men’s names (and foreign names) form the genitive with “lui” IN FRONT: “lui Radu”, “lui Vasile”. Women’s names in -a take -ei: “Ana” → “Anei”, “Nora” → “Norei”.

When something comes between the thing owned and the owner (an adjective, for example), or when the thing owned has no article, the possessive article appears: al, a, ai, ale. It agrees with the thing owned.
The same “al / a / ai / ale” also appears with possessives: “Al meu!” = “It’s mine!” (It’s mine, not yours.)
The dative shows to whom you give something (“to whom?”). It has the same endings as the genitive: -ului, -ei / -ii, -lor. The difference is the function: genitive = whose, dative = to whom.
I’m giving Ana a scarf. (to whom? to Ana)
I tell the children a story.
As with “pe” and direct pronouns, the short form is repeated here even when the name is there: “ÎI dau Anei”, “LE spun copiilor”.
The verb “a da” (to give) is irregular: dau, dai, dă, dăm, dați, dau.
The colour of the coat is green.
The children’s toys are on the floor.

I, Mițu, am an expert in clothes. I don’t wear them, of course. But I sleep on them. And I know exactly whose every thing in the house is, by its smell.
The grey jumper on the armchair is Mrs Pop’s. It smells of coffee and old books. The glasses on the table are hers too.
The blue jacket on the coat rack is Radu’s. It smells of rosin, that yellow powder for the violin bow. And of pretzels, because Radu always eats pretzels on the way.
The green coat is new. It’s Nora’s. It still smells of the shop, but from tomorrow it will smell of her: of mint tea and pencils.
But today I have a problem. On the red rug in Nora’s room there is a scarf I don’t know. A purple scarf, made of soft wool. It isn’t Mrs Pop’s. It isn’t Nora’s. It isn’t Radu’s either.
I sniff it. It smells of lilac perfume and of… fir trees? Who wears lilac perfume?
In the evening Nora comes home with Ana. Ana sees the scarf and cries: “My scarf! So this is where it was! I’ve been looking for it for a week!”
“It’s your scarf?” asks Nora. “You know, Mițu has been sleeping on it for three days.”
Ana laughs and takes it. “It’s my grandmother’s scarf. She made it herself, by hand, from the wool of the sheep in the village. For me it’s the most precious thing in my wardrobe.”
I look at Ana with big, sad eyes. That scarf was my best bed.
Ana bends down and strokes my head. “All right, all right, Mițu. Next time I’ll bring you a piece of grandma’s wool. Just for you.”
Then she turns to Nora: “And I’ll make you a scarf too, if you like. My grandmother is teaching me to knit. What colour do you like?”
“Red,” says Nora. “Like my rug. And like the roses…” Then she falls silent and blushes. Ana raises an eyebrow, exactly like Mrs Pop.
I don’t understand why people blush when they talk about roses. But I know one thing: in this house, everyone wants to give someone a present.
smell; to smell: eu miros (I smell)
the bow (the stick you play the violin with)
“la țară” = in the countryside, in the village
to teach: ea mă învață (she teaches me)
to knit: “să tricotez” (to make clothes from wool with needles)
to be silent: ea tace (she falls silent)

The “ia” is the traditional blouse of Romanian women.
It is white, made of linen or cotton, and has colourful embroidery on the sleeves and chest.
The colours and patterns of the embroidery differ from one region to another: red and black in Maramureș, blue in Oltenia, many colours in Bucovina.
Village women used to embroider the ia all winter long, by hand.
The ia has inspired many foreign artists. The French painter Henri Matisse has a famous painting: “The Romanian Blouse”.
On 24 June, Romanians celebrate Universal Day of the Ia. On that day many people wear an ia to the office or in the street.
linen, flax (a plant used to make cloth)
ie (the form of “ia” without the article)
